text: A force of 10N acts on a mass of 2kg. The acceleration produced is
explanation: Using F=ma: a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s².

text: The SI unit of force is the
explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), defined as the force needed to accelerate a 1kg mass at 1 m/s² (from F = ma).

text: Which of the following instruments is used to measure the diameter of a thin wire accurately?
explanation: The micrometer screw gauge measures very small lengths (down to 0.01mm) with high precision, ideal for thin wires, unlike less precise tools like the metre rule.

text: The fundamental quantities in physics include all of the following EXCEPT
explanation: Force is a derived quantity (from mass × acceleration); length, mass, and time are fundamental (base) quantities from which others are derived.

text: A vernier caliper has a zero error such that the reading is 0.02cm more than it should be. This is called a
explanation: When the zero mark of the vernier scale is to the right of the main scale zero (giving readings too high), this is a positive zero error, requiring the error to be subtracted.

text: The density of a substance is defined as its
explanation: Density (ρ) is defined as mass divided by volume (ρ = m/V), typically measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³.

text: Which of the following is a derived unit?
explanation: The Newton is derived from the base units kg, m, and s (kg·m/s²), unlike kilogram, metre, and ampere which are base SI units.

text: 1 micrometre is equal to
explanation: The prefix "micro" represents 10⁻⁶, so 1 micrometre (μm) = 10⁻⁶ metres.

text: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
explanation: Mass has magnitude only (no direction), making it a scalar quantity; the others (velocity, displacement, force) all require direction to be fully specified.

text: The instrument used to measure very small time intervals accurately, such as in a laboratory experiment, is the
explanation: A stopwatch provides precise measurement of short time intervals, often to a fraction of a second, essential in most physics experiments.

text: Which of the following represents a base quantity and its correct SI unit?
explanation: Time is a fundamental quantity with the SI base unit second (s); Force, Energy, and Pressure are derived quantities with corresponding derived units.

text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and a specific direction, making it a vector quantity, unlike speed, distance, and time which are scalars.

text: Two forces of 3N and 4N act at right angles to each other. The resultant force is
explanation: Using Pythagoras' theorem for perpendicular vectors: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5N.

text: The resultant of two forces acting in exactly opposite directions is found by
options: Subtracting the smaller from the larger
explanation: For collinear opposite forces, the resultant magnitude equals the difference between them, acting in the direction of the larger force.

text: Which method can be used to determine the resultant of two vectors acting at an angle to each other?
explanation: The parallelogram law states that the resultant of two vectors is represented by the diagonal of a parallelogram formed using the two vectors as adjacent sides.

text: A component of a vector is
options: Always equal to the vector itself
A part of the vector resolved along a specific direction (e.g., x or y axis)
explanation: Vector resolution breaks a single vector into perpendicular components (e.g., horizontal and vertical), which independently add up to reconstruct the original vector.

text: The rate of change of displacement with time is called
explanation: Velocity is precisely defined as the rate of change of displacement (a vector) with respect to time, distinguishing it from speed which is scalar.

text: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20m/s in 5 seconds. Its acceleration is
explanation: Acceleration = (v - u)/t = (20 - 0)/5 = 4 m/s².

text: Which of the following equations of motion correctly relates final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration and time?
explanation: v = u + at is the first standard equation of uniformly accelerated motion, derived directly from the definition of acceleration.

text: A body falling freely under gravity (ignoring air resistance) has an acceleration of approximately
explanation: The acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s² (sometimes approximated as 10 m/s² in calculations).

text: A body moves with uniform velocity when
options: Its speed changes at a constant rate
It covers equal displacements in equal time intervals, in the same direction
Its acceleration is constant but non-zero
explanation: Uniform velocity means both speed and direction remain constant, resulting in equal displacement covered in equal time intervals along a straight path.

text: The area under a velocity-time graph represents
explanation: Since velocity × time gives displacement, the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph numerically equals the displacement travelled.

text: The slope (gradient) of a distance-time graph gives
explanation: Speed is defined as distance divided by time, which corresponds exactly to the gradient of a distance-time graph.

text: A stone is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20m/s. Using g=10m/s², the time taken to reach maximum height is
explanation: At maximum height, final velocity = 0. Using v = u - gt: 0 = 20 - 10t, so t = 2s.

text: A car travels 100m in 20 seconds and then 150m in the next 30 seconds. Its average speed for the whole journey is
explanation: Total distance = 100+150 = 250m; total time = 20+30 = 50s. Average speed = 250/50 = 5 m/s.

text: Which of the following equations of motion is used to find displacement without needing time?
explanation: v² = u² + 2as directly relates initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, and displacement, without requiring time as a variable.

text: A body undergoing uniform acceleration starting from rest covers a distance of 40m in 4 seconds. The acceleration is
explanation: Using s = ut + ½at²: 40 = 0 + ½a(4)² = 8a, so a = 40/8 = 5 m/s².

text: Which of the following best describes projectile motion?
options: Motion in a straight line only
Motion under gravity alone, following a curved (parabolic) path
explanation: A projectile undergoes motion influenced only by gravity (ignoring air resistance), resulting in independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (accelerated) components that combine into a parabolic trajectory.

text: A ball is thrown horizontally from a height. Its horizontal velocity during flight (ignoring air resistance)
options: Becomes zero at the highest point
explanation: Since gravity acts only vertically, there is no horizontal force to change the horizontal velocity component, so it remains constant throughout the flight.

text: Retardation (deceleration) is best described as
options: Negative acceleration, i.e., a decrease in velocity with time
explanation: Retardation refers to acceleration acting in the opposite direction to motion, causing the velocity of a body to decrease over time.

text: A body moving in a circular path at constant speed has
options: Acceleration directed towards the centre (centripetal acceleration)
Acceleration directed away from the centre
explanation: Even at constant speed, the direction of velocity constantly changes in circular motion, producing centripetal acceleration directed toward the centre of the circle.

text: The formula for centripetal acceleration is
explanation: Centripetal acceleration is given by a = v²/r, where v is the linear speed and r is the radius of the circular path.

text: A train decelerates uniformly from 30m/s to rest over 100m. The deceleration is
Which type of motion is described by a straight, horizontal line on a velocity-time graph (not at zero)?
explanation: A horizontal line above the time axis on a velocity-time graph shows velocity is unchanging (zero acceleration) but non-zero, indicating uniform (constant) velocity.

text: The velocity of a body increases from 10m/s to 25m/s in 3 seconds. The acceleration is
explanation: Acceleration = (v-u)/t = (25-10)/3 = 15/3 = 5 m/s².

text: A body is said to be in equilibrium under motion when
options: The net force acting on it is zero, resulting in zero acceleration
explanation: Equilibrium (whether static or dynamic) requires the resultant of all forces acting to be zero, meaning the body has zero acceleration (constant velocity, possibly zero).

text: Newton's First Law of Motion states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless
options: Acted upon by an external unbalanced force
explanation: Newton's First Law (law of inertia) states an object maintains its state of rest or uniform velocity unless a net external force acts on it.

text: Newton's Second Law of Motion is mathematically expressed as
explanation: Newton's Second Law states force equals mass times acceleration (F=ma), showing force is directly proportional to both mass and acceleration.

text: Newton's Third Law states that
options: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Objects in motion remain in motion
Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions
explanation: For every action force exerted by one body on another, there is a simultaneous reaction force of equal magnitude but opposite direction on the first body.

text: The property of a body that resists changes in its state of motion is called
explanation: Inertia is the inherent resistance of a body (proportional to its mass) to changes in its velocity, whether starting, stopping, or changing direction.

text: Momentum is defined as the product of
explanation: Momentum (p) is defined as p = mv, the product of an object's mass and its velocity, and is a vector quantity.

text: The law of conservation of momentum states that in a closed system, the total momentum
options: Remains constant before and after collision, if no external force acts
explanation: In the absence of external forces, the total momentum of a system before a collision equals the total momentum after, whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.

text: A 2kg mass moving at 3m/s collides with a stationary 1kg mass, and they stick together. What is their common velocity after collision?
explanation: Momentum conservation: (2×3)+(1×0) = (2+1)×v → 6 = 3v → v = 2 m/s.

text: Weight of a body is defined as
options: The gravitational force acting on the body's mass
A scalar quantity with no direction
The same everywhere in the universe
explanation: Weight (W=mg) is the force exerted on a body's mass due to gravitational acceleration; unlike mass, it varies depending on the local gravitational field strength.

text: A 5kg object weighs approximately (using g=10m/s²)
explanation: Weight = mass × g = 5 × 10 = 50N.

text: In an elastic collision, which of the following is conserved?
explanation: Elastic collisions are defined as those in which both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved, unlike inelastic collisions where kinetic energy is lost (often to heat/sound).

text: Which of the following forces acts to oppose relative motion between two surfaces in contact?
explanation: Friction is the resistive force that opposes the relative sliding or tendency to slide between two surfaces in contact.

text: The impulse of a force is defined as the product of
explanation: Impulse (J = Ft) is the product of force and the time duration over which it acts, and it equals the change in momentum produced.

text: A rocket is propelled forward by expelling gases backward. This is best explained by
explanation: The backward expulsion of gas (action) produces an equal and opposite forward reaction force on the rocket, consistent with Newton's Third Law.

text: Which of the following reduces friction between moving parts of a machine?
explanation: Lubricants (like oil or grease) reduce direct contact between rough surfaces, thereby significantly reducing frictional resistance between moving machine parts.

text: The moment of a force about a point is defined as the product of
options: Force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
explanation: Moment (torque) = Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action, measured in Newton-metres (Nm).

text: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium
options: Total upward forces equal total downward forces only
Sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments about any point
There must be no forces acting
explanation: The principle of moments (for rotational equilibrium) requires that clockwise moments about a pivot exactly balance anticlockwise moments.

text: A uniform beam is balanced on a pivot. This point is called the
explanation: The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point about which a lever or beam rotates or balances.

text: For a body to be in complete (static) equilibrium, which conditions must be satisfied?
options: Net force is zero AND net moment (torque) about any point is zero
The body must be at rest permanently
explanation: Complete equilibrium requires both translational equilibrium (net force = 0) and rotational equilibrium (net moment = 0).

text: A force of 20N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.5m from a pivot. The moment produced is
explanation: Moment = Force × perpendicular distance = 20 × 0.5 = 10 Nm.

text: The centre of gravity of a uniform rectangular lamina is located
options: At the intersection of its diagonals
explanation: For a symmetric uniform lamina like a rectangle, the centre of gravity lies at the geometric centre, found at the intersection point of the diagonals.

text: A see-saw is balanced when a 40kg child sits 2m from the pivot on one side. Where must a 50kg child sit on the other side to balance it?
explanation: Using principle of moments: 40×2 = 50×d → d = 80/50 = 1.6m.

text: A body is in stable equilibrium if, when slightly displaced, it
explanation: Stable equilibrium is characterized by a restoring tendency — when displaced slightly, the body's centre of gravity creates a moment that returns it to the original position.

text: A ladder resting against a smooth wall and on a rough floor remains in equilibrium mainly due to
options: Balanced forces including friction at the floor and normal reactions at wall and floor
Zero net force at the wall
explanation: Equilibrium of the ladder depends on balancing the weight, the normal reaction from the wall, the normal reaction from the floor, and frictional force at the floor preventing slipping.

text: Which of the following is an example of a couple?
options: A single force acting on a body
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces acting on a body along different lines of action, producing rotation
Two forces cancelling each other exactly at the same point
explanation: A couple consists of two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide, producing a turning effect (pure rotation) without net translational force.

text: Work done is defined as the product of
options: Force and displacement in the direction of the force
explanation: Work (W = Fs cosθ) is done when a force causes displacement, specifically the component of force acting along the direction of motion multiplied by the displacement.

text: The SI unit of energy is the
explanation: Energy (and work) is measured in Joules (J), where 1 Joule equals the work done when a force of 1N moves an object 1m in the force's direction.

text: Power is defined as the rate of
options: Doing work (energy transferred per unit time)
explanation: Power (P = W/t) measures how quickly work is done or energy is transferred, measured in Watts (Joules per second).

text: The law of conservation of energy states that energy
options: Can be created but not destroyed
Can be destroyed but not created
Can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another
explanation: This fundamental law states total energy in an isolated system remains constant, though it changes forms (e.g., kinetic to potential), such as in a swinging pendulum.

text: Kinetic energy of a moving body is given by
explanation: Kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²) is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion, depending on both its mass and the square of its velocity.

text: Potential energy due to position (gravitational) is given by
explanation: Gravitational potential energy (PE = mgh) depends on an object's mass, the gravitational field strength, and its height above a reference level.

text: A 2kg object is raised to a height of 5m. Using g=10m/s², its potential energy gained is
A machine does 500J of work in 10 seconds. Its power output is
explanation: Power = Work/time = 500/10 = 50 W.

text: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
explanation: Solar energy is continuously replenished by the sun and does not deplete with use, unlike fossil fuels (coal, gas, petroleum) which are finite, non-renewable resources.

text: Mechanical energy is the sum of
explanation: Mechanical energy is defined as the total of an object's kinetic energy (due to motion) and potential energy (due to position or state).

text: A car engine converts chemical energy in fuel into which form of energy to move the car?
explanation: Combustion of fuel releases chemical energy, which is converted (via the engine) primarily into mechanical energy to drive the car's motion.

text: A pendulum bob at its highest point has
options: Maximum kinetic energy and zero potential energy
Maximum potential energy and zero (or minimum) kinetic energy
explanation: At the highest point of a swing, the bob is momentarily at rest (zero velocity, minimum KE), while it is at its greatest height (maximum PE).

text: 1 horsepower is approximately equal to
explanation: The horsepower is a traditional unit of power, with 1 hp defined as approximately 746 Watts.

text: Efficiency of a machine is defined as
options: Input energy divided by output energy
Useful output energy (or work) divided by total input energy, expressed as a percentage
explanation: Efficiency = (useful output/total input) × 100%, indicating how effectively a machine converts input energy into useful work, always less than 100% due to energy losses.

text: A ball dropped from a height loses potential energy which is converted mainly into
options: Kinetic energy (as it falls, ignoring air resistance)
explanation: As the ball falls, its height (and potential energy) decreases while its speed (and kinetic energy) increases, in accordance with the conservation of mechanical energy.

text: The mechanical advantage of a machine is defined as
options: Distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load
explanation: Mechanical advantage (MA) = Load/Effort, representing how much the machine multiplies the input effort force.

text: The velocity ratio of a machine is defined as
options: Distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load
explanation: Velocity ratio (VR) compares how far the effort moves compared to how far the load moves in the same time, and depends only on the machine's geometry.

text: In an ideal (perfectly efficient) machine, mechanical advantage is
explanation: For a perfectly efficient (ideal) machine with no energy losses, MA equals VR, giving 100% efficiency; in real machines, MA is always less than VR due to friction.

text: A lever with the fulcrum between the load and effort is classified as
explanation: In a first-class lever (e.g., see-saw, scissors), the fulcrum sits between the effort and load, unlike second-class (load between fulcrum and effort, e.g., wheelbarrow) or third-class levers.

text: An example of a second-class lever is
explanation: In a wheelbarrow, the load lies between the fulcrum (wheel) and the effort (handles), characteristic of a second-class lever.

text: A pulley system has a velocity ratio of 4. If a load of 200N is lifted with an effort of 60N, the efficiency is
The inclined plane is a simple machine that makes work easier by
options: Reducing the effort needed to raise a load, though over a longer distance
explanation: An inclined plane trades distance for reduced effort — the load is raised using less force but the effort must move a greater distance along the slope.

text: In a screw jack, the velocity ratio is given by
options: Circumference of the handle's circular path ÷ pitch of the screw
Pitch of the screw ÷ length of the handle
explanation: For a screw jack, VR = (2πR)/pitch, where R is the length of the handle (radius of the circular path) and pitch is the distance advanced per revolution.

text: Which of the following increases the mechanical advantage of a pulley system?
options: Increasing the number of pulleys used to support the load
explanation: Adding more pulleys (and supporting strings) in a block-and-tackle system increases the velocity ratio and, correspondingly, the mechanical advantage achievable.

text: The efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100% mainly because of
options: Energy losses due to friction and other resistive forces
The velocity ratio being too high
explanation: In practice, some input energy is always lost overcoming friction (and other resistances) and converted to heat, meaning not all input energy becomes useful output, so efficiency is always below 100%.

text: Heat energy always flows from a body at
explanation: By the second law of thermodynamics, heat naturally flows from regions of higher temperature to lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached.

text: The SI unit of temperature is the
explanation: Kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, with 0K representing absolute zero, the theoretical point of zero molecular motion.

text: The specific heat capacity of a substance is defined as the heat energy needed to raise the temperature of
options: Any mass of the substance by 100°C
explanation: Specific heat capacity (c) is defined as the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of a unit mass (1kg) of a substance by 1 degree (Celsius or Kelvin).

text: The heat required to change a substance from solid to liquid at constant temperature is called
explanation: Latent heat of fusion is the energy absorbed to convert a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point, without any change in temperature.

text: Heat transfer through a solid medium without bulk movement of the material is called
explanation: Conduction transfers heat through direct molecular vibration and electron movement within a solid, without any physical movement of the material itself.

text: Convection as a mode of heat transfer occurs mainly in
explanation: Convection involves the bulk movement of heated fluid particles (liquids or gases) carrying thermal energy, a process not possible in rigid solids.

text: Which mode of heat transfer does NOT require a material medium?
explanation: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves and can travel through a vacuum, unlike conduction and convection which require a material medium.

text: 500g of water is heated, raising its temperature by 10°C. If the specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C, the heat absorbed is
The process by which a liquid changes to vapor below its boiling point is called
explanation: Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid at any temperature below boiling point, as higher-energy molecules escape into the vapor phase.

text: When a gas is compressed suddenly, its temperature
explanation: Sudden compression does work on the gas, increasing the internal (kinetic) energy of its molecules, and thus raising its temperature (as in a bicycle pump warming up).

text: Linear expansivity of a solid is defined as the increase in length per unit original length per
explanation: Linear expansivity (α) measures the fractional increase in length of a solid per degree rise in temperature, used to predict thermal expansion in structures like railway tracks and bridges.

text: Why are gaps left between railway tracks?
options: To reduce the cost of materials
To allow for thermal expansion of the metal on hot days
explanation: Metal rails expand when heated; gaps prevent the tracks from buckling or warping due to thermal expansion during hot weather.

text: The transfer of heat energy by electromagnetic waves is called
explanation: Radiation is heat transfer via electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared), requiring no medium, as demonstrated by heat reaching Earth from the sun through the vacuum of space.

text: A thermometer works based on the principle that
options: All liquids boil at the same temperature
Substances (like mercury) expand predictably with an increase in temperature
explanation: Liquid-in-glass thermometers rely on the consistent, measurable expansion of a liquid (e.g., mercury or alcohol) with rising temperature to indicate a temperature value.

text: Which temperature scale sets 0° as the freezing point and 100° as the boiling point of water at standard pressure?
explanation: The Celsius scale is defined with water's freezing point at 0°C and boiling point at 100°C under standard atmospheric pressure.

text: A wave is best described as
options: A movement of matter from one place to another
A disturbance that transfers energy from one point to another without the net transfer of matter
A form of matter with mass
explanation: Waves transport energy through a medium (or vacuum, for EM waves) via oscillations, without the medium's particles undergoing net displacement in the direction of wave travel.

text: The distance between two successive crests of a wave is called
explanation: Wavelength (λ) is defined as the distance between two consecutive points in phase, such as successive crests or troughs of a wave.

text: In a transverse wave, particle vibration is
options: Parallel to the direction of wave travel
Perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
In circles around the direction of travel
explanation: In transverse waves (e.g., light, water waves), particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy/wave propagation.

text: In a longitudinal wave, particle vibration is
options: Perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
Parallel to the direction of wave travel
explanation: In longitudinal waves (e.g., sound), particles vibrate back and forth along the same direction the wave travels, creating compressions and rarefactions.

text: A wave with frequency 50Hz and wavelength 2m travels at a speed of
The number of complete waves passing a point per second is called the
explanation: Frequency (f) is defined as the number of complete oscillations (or wave cycles) occurring per unit time, measured in Hertz (Hz).

text: The time taken for one complete oscillation of a wave is called its
explanation: The period (T) is the time for one full cycle of oscillation, related to frequency by T = 1/f.

text: Which of the following is an example of electromagnetic waves?
explanation: Light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, capable of travelling through a vacuum, unlike sound, water, and seismic waves which require a material medium.

text: The phenomenon where a wave bends around obstacles or spreads out after passing through a narrow gap is called
explanation: Diffraction refers specifically to the bending/spreading of waves around obstacles or through apertures, most noticeable when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength.

text: Sound waves are classified as
explanation: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave, with air particles vibrating parallel to the direction of wave propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions.

text: Sound cannot travel through
explanation: Sound requires a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate via particle vibrations; it cannot travel through the vacuum of space, unlike light.

text: The speed of sound is generally greatest in
explanation: Sound travels fastest through solids due to closely packed particles allowing rapid transmission of vibrations, followed by liquids, then gases.

text: The loudness of a sound is mainly determined by its
explanation: Loudness corresponds to the amplitude (energy) of the sound wave — larger amplitude vibrations produce louder sounds.

text: The pitch of a sound is determined mainly by its
explanation: Pitch is directly related to frequency — higher frequency sound waves are perceived as higher pitched notes.

text: An echo is produced due to
options: Reflection of sound waves off a hard surface
explanation: An echo occurs when sound waves reflect off a hard, distant surface and return to the listener after a detectable time delay.

text: The human ear can normally detect sound frequencies within the range of
explanation: The typical audible range for humans is 20Hz (lower limit) to 20,000Hz (upper limit); sounds outside this range (infrasound/ultrasound) are inaudible to humans.

text: Sound waves with frequency above the audible human range are called
explanation: Ultrasonic waves have frequencies above 20,000Hz, beyond human hearing range, but are used in applications like medical imaging and sonar.

text: Resonance occurs when a body vibrates at its
options: Natural frequency, driven by an external force of the same frequency
explanation: Resonance happens when an object is driven by an external periodic force matching its natural frequency, causing a dramatic increase in amplitude of vibration.

text: The minimum time interval required for a human to distinguish an echo from the original sound is approximately
explanation: A time gap of at least about 0.1 seconds is generally needed for the human ear to perceive the reflected sound as a distinct echo rather than a continuation of the original sound.

text: The law of reflection states that
options: The angle of incidence is always greater than the angle of reflection
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both lie in the same plane
Light always bends towards the normal
explanation: The law of reflection states the incident and reflected rays make equal angles with the normal at the point of incidence, and both lie in the same plane.

text: A real image is one that
options: Can be seen on a screen, formed by actual convergence of light rays
Cannot be projected onto a screen
Is always smaller than the object
explanation: Real images form where light rays actually converge and can be captured/projected on a screen, unlike virtual images which appear to originate from a point but involve no actual convergence.

text: A concave mirror can form a virtual image when the object is placed
options: Between the pole and the focus
explanation: When an object is placed between the pole and focal point of a concave mirror, the reflected rays diverge, appearing to originate from behind the mirror, forming a magnified virtual image.

text: The refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of
options: Speed of light in vacuum to speed of light in the medium
Speed of light in the medium to speed of light in vacuum
Angle of incidence to angle of refraction only
explanation: Refractive index (n) = speed of light in vacuum/speed of light in medium, indicating how much light slows down when entering the medium.

text: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a
options: Less dense to a denser medium at any angle
Denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
Denser to a less dense medium at any angle
explanation: Total internal reflection requires light moving from a denser to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for all light to be reflected internally.

text: A convex lens is also known as a
explanation: A convex lens causes parallel light rays to converge to a focal point after refraction, hence its designation as a converging lens.

text: The image formed by a plane mirror is
options: Real, inverted, and same size as object
Virtual, upright, and same size as object (laterally inverted)
explanation: A plane mirror always forms a virtual, upright image of the same size as the object, though laterally inverted (left-right reversed).

text: Which lens is used to correct short-sightedness (myopia)?
explanation: Myopia occurs because the eye focuses images in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens spreads out light rays before entering the eye, moving the focal point back onto the retina.

text: Which lens is used to correct long-sightedness (hypermetropia)?
explanation: Hypermetropia occurs when the eye focuses images behind the retina; a converging (convex) lens brings the focal point forward onto the retina.

text: The splitting of white light into its component colours by a prism is called
explanation: Dispersion occurs because different colours (wavelengths) of light refract by slightly different amounts passing through a prism, spreading white light into a spectrum.

text: The order of colours in the visible spectrum, from longest to shortest wavelength, is
options: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet
Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Indigo, Orange
Blue, Green, Red, Yellow, Violet, Orange, Indigo
explanation: The visible spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength follows red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV), with red having the longest wavelength.

text: A ray of light passing through the optical centre of a lens
explanation: A ray passing through the optical centre of a thin lens travels in a straight line without bending, a key property used in ray diagram constructions.

text: The focal length of a mirror is related to its radius of curvature by
explanation: For spherical mirrors, the focal length equals half the radius of curvature (f = R/2), a standard relationship in mirror optics.

text: A camera and the human eye are similar in that both use a
options: Concave mirror to form real images
Convex lens to form real, inverted images on a light-sensitive surface
Plane mirror to form virtual images
explanation: Both the camera (using its lens and film/sensor) and the eye (using its lens and retina) form real, inverted images using a convex lens system.

text: The critical angle is defined as the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is
explanation: The critical angle is specifically the angle of incidence at which the refracted ray travels exactly along the boundary of the two media, i.e., at 90° to the normal.

text: Like charges
options: Have no effect on each other
explanation: Fundamental to electrostatics, charges of the same sign (both positive or both negative) exert a repulsive force on each other.

text: The process by which an object becomes charged without direct contact, due to a nearby charged object, is called
explanation: Electrostatic induction occurs when a charged object causes redistribution of charge in a nearby neutral conductor without direct physical contact.

text: Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is
options: Directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
Inversely proportional to the product of the charges
Directly proportional to the distance between them
explanation: Coulomb's Law: F = kq₁q₂/r², showing force increases with charge magnitude but decreases rapidly (inverse square) with increasing separation distance.

text: An electroscope is used to
options: Detect and test the presence and sign of electric charge
explanation: A gold-leaf electroscope detects the presence of static charge and can help determine whether a charge is positive or negative through the divergence of its leaves.

text: Electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge point
options: Away from the charge, radially outward
explanation: By convention, electric field lines originate from positive charges and point radially outward, indicating the direction a positive test charge would move.

text: The unit of electric charge is the
explanation: Electric charge is measured in Coulombs (C), where 1 Coulomb is the quantity of charge transported by a current of 1 Ampere in 1 second.

text: Charging by friction typically involves the transfer of
explanation: When two different materials are rubbed together, electrons (the most mobile charged particles) are transferred from one surface to the other, leaving one object positively charged and the other negatively charged.

text: A conductor differs from an insulator in that a conductor
options: Allows free movement of charge (electrons) through it
explanation: Conductors contain free (delocalized) electrons that can move readily through the material, allowing charge to flow, unlike insulators where electrons are tightly bound.

text: The lightning conductor on tall buildings works by
options: Attracting lightning and storing its charge permanently
Providing a safe, low-resistance path for charge to safely reach the ground
Insulating the building from all charge
explanation: A lightning conductor (typically a metal rod connected to earth) provides a preferred low-resistance path, safely conducting the massive discharge current to the ground, protecting the building.

text: Two point charges of +4μC and +2μC are placed 3m apart. Which statement about the force between them is correct?
options: There is no force between them
The force is zero because both charges are small
explanation: Since both charges are positive (like charges), the electrostatic force between them is repulsive, in accordance with Coulomb's Law.

text: Electric current is defined as the rate of flow of
explanation: Current (I = Q/t) is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit, measured in Amperes.

text: Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor is
options: Directly proportional to voltage, at constant temperature
explanation: Ohm's Law (V=IR) states that at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to the potential difference (voltage) across a conductor.

text: The SI unit of electrical resistance is the
explanation: Resistance is measured in Ohms (Ω), defined via Ohm's Law as V/I.

text: A current of 2A flows through a resistor for 5 seconds. The total charge that flows is
explanation: Q = It = 2 × 5 = 10 Coulombs.

text: For resistors connected in series, the total resistance is
options: Less than the smallest individual resistance
Equal to the largest resistance only
explanation: In series circuits, resistances simply add up: R(total) = R1 + R2 + R3 + ..., since the same current flows through each resistor sequentially.

text: For resistors connected in parallel, the reciprocal of total resistance equals
options: The sum of the individual resistances
The sum of the reciprocals of individual resistances
explanation: In parallel: 1/R(total) = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ..., because the voltage across each branch is equal but current splits among branches.

text: Two resistors of 4Ω and 6Ω are connected in series to a 12V battery. The current flowing is
explanation: Total resistance = 4+6 = 10Ω. Current = V/R = 12/10 = 1.2A.

text: Electrical power dissipated in a resistor is given by
explanation: Electrical power is given by P = VI (also expressible as P=I²R or P=V²/R using Ohm's Law substitutions).

text: A device rated 100W operating at 220V draws a current of
explanation: Using P=VI: I = P/V = 100/220 ≈ 0.45A.

text: An ammeter is connected in _____ in a circuit to measure current.
explanation: An ammeter must be connected in series so that the full circuit current flows directly through it for accurate measurement; it has very low resistance to avoid affecting the circuit.

text: A voltmeter is connected in _____ across a component to measure potential difference.
options: It cannot be connected in a circuit
explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component, and has very high resistance to draw minimal current, allowing accurate measurement of the potential difference.

text: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary coil and 500 turns on the secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 20V, the secondary voltage is
The electromotive force (EMF) of a cell is defined as
options: The voltage lost due to internal resistance
The total energy supplied per unit charge by the source, including energy lost to internal resistance
The current supplied by the cell
The resistance of the external circuit
explanation: EMF represents the total electrical energy the source provides per coulomb of charge, encompassing both the terminal (external) voltage and the voltage drop due to internal resistance.

text: A wire's resistance is directly proportional to its
explanation: Resistance (R = ρL/A) increases directly with the length of the wire, since a longer conductor offers a greater path of resistance to current flow.

text: Which of the following materials is the best electrical conductor?
explanation: Copper has an abundance of free electrons and very low resistivity, making it an excellent conductor commonly used in electrical wiring.

text: The heating effect of an electric current is utilized in
explanation: Devices like electric heaters and kettles rely on the heating (Joule) effect, where electrical energy is converted directly to heat as current flows through a resistive element.

text: A fuse in an electrical circuit works by
options: Melting and breaking the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit
explanation: A fuse contains a thin wire that melts (breaking the circuit) when current exceeds its rated value, protecting the circuit and appliances from damage due to excessive current.

text: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of
explanation: The kilowatt-hour measures energy (Power × time), commonly used by electricity providers to bill consumers for total electrical energy consumed.

text: Three resistors of 2Ω each are connected in parallel. The total resistance is
Internal resistance of a cell causes
options: An increase in terminal voltage as current increases
A decrease (drop) in terminal voltage as current drawn increases
explanation: As more current is drawn, more voltage is "lost" across the cell's internal resistance (V=EMF−Ir), reducing the terminal voltage available to the external circuit.

text: Which of the following best explains why electrical wires are often made of copper rather than iron?
options: Copper has lower resistivity, making it a more efficient conductor
Iron does not conduct electricity at all
explanation: Copper has significantly lower electrical resistivity than iron, allowing more efficient current flow with less energy loss as heat, making it preferable for wiring despite higher cost.

text: Like magnetic poles
explanation: Similar to electric charges, like magnetic poles (N-N or S-S) repel each other, while unlike poles (N-S) attract.

text: A magnetic field is best represented using
options: Magnetic field lines/lines of force, from North to South pole outside the magnet
Straight lines only, with no direction
explanation: Magnetic field lines conventionally emerge from the North pole and enter the South pole (externally), forming closed loops representing field direction and relative strength.

text: A material that can be strongly magnetized and retains its magnetism is called a
explanation: Hard magnetic materials (e.g., steel) retain magnetization well after the magnetizing field is removed, making them suitable for permanent magnets, unlike soft magnetic materials (e.g., iron) which lose magnetism quickly.

text: The magnetic effect of an electric current was first discovered by
explanation: Oersted discovered in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle, demonstrating that electric currents produce magnetic fields.

text: An electromagnet's strength can be increased by
options: Decreasing the number of turns in the coil
Increasing the current and the number of turns, and using a soft iron core
explanation: Electromagnet strength increases with higher current, more coil turns, and use of a soft iron core (which is easily magnetized and demagnetized), all boosting the magnetic field produced.

text: Electromagnetic induction refers to the production of
options: A magnetic field from a stationary charge
An induced EMF (and current) due to a changing magnetic field or relative motion between a conductor and magnetic field
explanation: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit (from relative motion or changing current) induces an EMF and current in that circuit.

text: Lenz's Law states that the direction of an induced current is such that it
options: Supports the change that produced it
Opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
Is always in the same direction as the inducing current
explanation: Lenz's Law (a consequence of energy conservation) states induced current flows in a direction that creates a magnetic field opposing the original change in flux that caused it.

text: A transformer works on the principle of
options: Mutual electromagnetic induction between primary and secondary coils
explanation: Transformers use a changing current in the primary coil to produce a changing magnetic flux, which induces an EMF in the secondary coil via mutual induction.

text: A step-up transformer
options: Increases voltage and decreases current (assuming ideal, no power loss)
explanation: A step-up transformer has more secondary turns than primary turns, increasing output voltage while proportionally decreasing current to conserve power (Vp·Ip = Vs·Is, ideally).

text: The right-hand grip rule is used to determine the direction of
options: The magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor
explanation: The right-hand grip rule states that if the thumb points in the direction of conventional current flow, the curled fingers indicate the direction of the magnetic field around the conductor.

text: A simple electric motor converts
options: Chemical energy to electrical energy directly
explanation: An electric motor uses the force experienced by a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field (motor effect) to convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy.

text: A simple AC generator (dynamo) converts
explanation: A generator uses electromagnetic induction, rotating a coil within a magnetic field (mechanical input) to induce an alternating EMF (electrical output).

text: Which material is best suited as the core of a transformer?
explanation: Soft iron is easily magnetized and demagnetized (low magnetic retentivity/hysteresis loss), making it ideal for efficiently channeling changing magnetic flux in a transformer core.

text: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is given by
explanation: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor is F = BIL sinθ, where B is magnetic flux density, I is current, L is conductor length in the field, and θ is the angle between current direction and field.

text: A diode is a device that allows current to flow
explanation: A diode is a semiconductor device that permits current flow in one direction only (forward bias), blocking flow in the reverse direction, making it useful for rectification.

text: The process of converting alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) is called
explanation: Rectification, typically using diodes, converts the bidirectional flow of AC into a unidirectional flow characteristic of DC.

text: A transistor is mainly used in electronic circuits for
options: Amplification and switching of electronic signals
explanation: Transistors are versatile semiconductor devices widely used to amplify weak signals or act as electronic switches in circuits.

text: Which of these is a semiconductor material commonly used in electronic devices?
explanation: Silicon is a widely used semiconductor material, forming the basis of diodes, transistors, and integrated circuits due to its intermediate electrical conductivity that can be precisely controlled.

text: In an AC supply, the frequency in Nigeria (and most of the world) is standardized at
explanation: Nigeria's national grid, like much of Africa, Europe, and Asia, operates at a standard AC frequency of 50Hz (compared to 60Hz used in the USA and parts of the Americas).

text: An atom consists mainly of
options: A dense positive nucleus surrounded by orbiting negative electrons
explanation: The nuclear model of the atom describes a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons occupying much larger orbital regions.

text: Radioactivity is the spontaneous
options: Disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei, emitting radiation
Absorption of light by an atom
explanation: Radioactivity refers to the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, releasing energy in the form of alpha, beta, or gamma radiation to achieve a more stable state.

text: An alpha particle is equivalent to
options: A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons)
explanation: An alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons bound together, identical in composition to a helium-4 nucleus, and carries a +2 charge.

text: A beta particle emitted during radioactive decay is essentially
explanation: Beta decay involves a neutron converting to a proton (or vice versa) within the nucleus, emitting a high-speed electron (beta particle) in the process.

text: Which type of radioactive emission has the greatest penetrating power?
explanation: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation with the greatest penetrating power, capable of passing through several centimetres of lead, unlike alpha (stopped by paper) or beta (stopped by thin metal) particles.

text: The half-life of a radioactive substance is defined as the time taken for
options: All the substance to decay completely
Half of the original number of radioactive nuclei to decay
The substance to double in mass
The substance to become stable permanently at once
explanation: Half-life is a statistical measure representing the time required for exactly half of a sample of radioactive nuclei to undergo decay, a constant characteristic of each isotope.

text: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 4 days. After 12 days, the fraction of the original sample remaining is
explanation: 12 days represents 3 half-lives (12/4=3). Remaining fraction = (1/2)³ = 1/8.

text: Nuclear fission involves
options: The combination of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy
The emission of a single electron from an atom
explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g., Uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing significant energy, as utilized in nuclear power plants.

text: Nuclear fusion is the process by which
options: Heavy nuclei split into lighter ones
Light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
Electrons are emitted from an atom
explanation: Fusion combines light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) under extreme conditions (as in stars) to form heavier nuclei, releasing enormous amounts of energy.

text: X-rays are produced when
options: Fast-moving electrons are suddenly decelerated upon striking a metal target
A magnet is moved near a coil
Radioactive decay occurs naturally without any external trigger
explanation: X-rays are generated in an X-ray tube when high-speed electrons are abruptly decelerated (or deflected) upon collision with a dense metal target, converting kinetic energy into electromagnetic radiation.

text: Pressure is defined as
explanation: Pressure (P = F/A) is defined as the force acting perpendicularly per unit area, measured in Pascals (N/m²).

text: According to Pascal's principle, pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is
options: Absorbed entirely at the point of application
Transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid
Only transmitted downward due to gravity
explanation: Pascal's Principle states that pressure applied to a confined, incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished and equally throughout the entire fluid, forming the basis of hydraulic systems.

text: A hydraulic press works based on the principle that
options: A small force on a small piston can produce a much larger force on a larger piston, since pressure is equal throughout the fluid
Force is lost as it travels through the fluid
Only large pistons can generate pressure
explanation: Since pressure (F/A) is equal throughout the connected fluid, a small force applied to a small-area piston produces the same pressure that, acting over a much larger piston area, yields a much greater output force.

text: Atmospheric pressure is measured using a
explanation: A barometer (e.g., mercury barometer) measures atmospheric pressure based on the height of a liquid column it can support against the pressure of the atmosphere.

text: According to Archimedes' Principle, the upthrust (buoyant force) on a body submerged in a fluid equals
options: The weight of the body itself
The weight of the fluid displaced by the body
The density of the fluid only
explanation: Archimedes' Principle states that the buoyant force experienced by a submerged (or floating) object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces, explaining why objects float or sink.

text: The wave equation relating speed, frequency, and wavelength is
explanation: Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength (v = fλ), a fundamental relationship applicable to all wave types.
